hints: A company connects all of its cities, but creating every pair of connections is too expensive.
Introduce one extra node per company.
Pay the ticket cost when entering that company node and zero when leaving it.
analogy: Each company is a hub: buying its ticket lets you exit at any city it serves.
example: If company A serves cities 1 and 3 for 4, and company B serves 3 and 2 for 2, the cheapest cost from 1 to 2 is 6.
algorithm: Create a directed graph with a node for each city and each company. For every city served by company i, add city->company with weight c[i] and company->city with weight 0. Run Dijkstra from city 1 and output distances of the city nodes.
correctness: A city-company-city step costs exactly one ticket and can reach any city served by that company. Every actual itinerary maps to an equal-cost path in the expanded graph, and every expanded path describes valid ticket purchases. Dijkstra finds the cheapest path because all costs are nonnegative.
complexity: With n cities, m companies and K total city memberships, the graph has n+m vertices and 2K edges. Dijkstra takes O((n+m+K) log(n+m)) time and O(n+m+K) space.
